pages.x: In the first cities of Sumer, in what is now southern Iraq, temples collected grain, beer, sheep and cloth. To keep track, officials used small clay tokens, then pressed marks into clay tablets: a picture of an ear of barley, and strokes for the numbers. Writing began as bookkeeping.
Scribes learned to use a sign for its sound as well as its meaning, like a rebus: in Sumerian the arrow and the word for life were both "ti", so the arrow sign could write life.
pages.fx: Now writing could record anything people said, such as names, laws, letters, prayers and stories, not only lists of goods.

pages.x: Scribes wrote by pressing a cut reed into wet clay, leaving wedge shapes we call cuneiform, from the Latin for wedge. Clay was cheap and it lasted: when a palace library burned, the fire baked its tablets hard. Cuneiform was used for 3,000 years and for more than a dozen languages.

Writing appeared in Egypt at about the same time, perhaps inspired by Sumer, perhaps not. Hieroglyphs, pictures standing for sounds and ideas, were carved on temples and tombs for over 3,000 years. Later, people in China and in Mexico invented writing again, on their own.

pages.t: The first author with a name
pages.x: Enheduanna, daughter of King Sargon of Akkad, was high priestess of the moon god at Ur around 2300 BC. She wrote hymns to the goddess Inanna and put her own name to them, which makes her the first author in history we know by name.

Scribes were trained in "tablet houses". A Sumerian school story tells of a pupil who was caned for talking, for standing up, for walking out of the gate and for bad handwriting. That evening his father invited the teacher home for dinner and gave him a present, and the beatings stopped.

Written in cuneiform, the epic tells of Gilgamesh, a king of Uruk who searches for a way to escape death. It has a great flood, a man who survives it in a boat full of animals, and a snake that steals the plant of youth. It is the oldest great story to survive.

Writing let knowledge outlive the people who had it. Laws could be fixed, letters sent, stories kept and the past recorded, which is why the time before writing is called prehistory. The letters you are reading go back, through the Greeks and Phoenicians, to signs first drawn in Egypt.
